_doc: ONE RULE, THREE PORTS. This is the table each client's credential probe is asserted against:
given the HTTP status Lens returns from GET /v1/auth/me, what may the client conclude about the
It exists because the three clients previously concluded NOTHING — every one of them tested the
connection with an unauthenticated GET /healthz and reported success, so a wrong, revoked or
expired key produced a green tick in VS Code, in the JetBrains plugin and from `talyvor-code
check`. Adding an authenticated probe to three runtimes independently is exactly how the three
safeurl ports came to disagree on 6 of 29 cases; this file is the same remedy.
THE RULE IS FAIL-OPEN AND THAT IS THE POINT: only an explicit 401 or 403 is a verdict against
the key. Everything else is 'unknown', which the caller must report as it reported before this
probe existed. A 404 means an older Lens without the route; 5xx means a degraded Lens; 4xx
otherwise means the probe itself was wrong. None of those is evidence the key is bad, and
reporting them as bad would red a working install.
NOT IN THE TABLE, DELIBERATELY: 3xx. Every one of these three runtimes follows redirects by
default and each follows a different number of them, so a 3xx row would assert the HTTP client's
redirect policy rather than this rule — the shape the safeurl table hit when Node kept IPv6
brackets and Go did not. A redirect that terminates lands on one of the rows below.

cases.why: no body is still an authenticated answer
the 2xx class is the boundary, not the listed codes
the key is wrong, revoked or expired
the key authenticates but is not permitted here — still the key, not the URL
the probe was malformed; says nothing about the key
an older Lens with no /v1/auth/me route
a proxy that refuses GET on this path
rate limited — the key may be perfectly good
a gateway in front of Lens; the request never arrived
